<Rep. Frank Pallone, Jr.>: We oppose H.R. 6373, the ``Air Permitting Improvements to Protect National Security Act of 2025,'' which allows the President to exempt certain polluting facilities from Clean Air Act (CAA) requirements, under the undefined guise of a ``national security interest.'' The bill would also set up a pay-to-play scheme allowing certain polluting facilities to pay state regulators a nominal fee in lieu of controlling their harmful pollution.
BACKGROUND
The CAA requires the owner or operator of any new or expanded source of air pollution to obtain permits before construction begins, ensuring that new and expanding facilities will not increase pollution above levels that are safe to breathe. The preconstruction permitting provisions achieve this by requiring new and modified sources to use control technology to reduce their emissions; and to assess, and if necessary, address their remaining air quality impacts. This approach ensures that both the facility and community can mitigate any pollution increases before building begins, when it is most cost-effective.
EPA's New Source Review (NSR) program includes three different types of permitting requirements that depend on the size of a facility and the air quality where the facility will be located. For nonattainment areas, which already have dangerous, unhealthy air, the facility owner or operator must obtain a preconstruction permit under the nonattainment NSR program. CAA Section 173 permits require the installation of pollution controls that are sufficient to meet the lowest achievable emission rate, emission offsets from existing sources, and the opportunity for public involvement.\1\
\1\42 U.S.C. Sec. 7503.
The majority claims that permitting delays have stalled key projects, and provisions of this bill will help onshore key industries. However, they offered no specific examples of stalled projects during the hearings, markups, or in their report. They produced no justification for providing sweeping exemptions from critical public health safeguards, nor any explanation for giving the President the ability to waive CAA requirements for favored industrial polluters, as H.R. 6373 would do.
SUMMARY OF H.R. 6373
Section 2(1) amends CAA Section 173 to allow the President to issue a waiver to an owner or operator of a new or modified advanced manufacturing facility, or critical mineral facility, for any required offset of its air pollution. This section is harmful to public health and will lead to increases in emissions of cancer-causing pollution in communities. This section also creates an unfair scheme where those who get a waiver are given a free pass to ratchet up pollution, and other facilities will need to cut more pollution to make up the difference. Other industries, and the states and counties where they are located, will be punished by these waivers because they will have to do more, likely at higher cost, to ensure healthy air quality.
During the Environment Subcommittee markup, the majority rejected a simple anti-corruption amendment to ensure that these national security waivers would not be used to bestow preferential treatment on Trump Administration friends and favored entities. An amendment to ensure this act would not increase health harms in vulnerable communities was also rejected by the majority.
Section 2(2) amends CAA Section 173 to create a pay-to-play scheme in which facilities can pay state regulators 1.5 times the average cost of emissions reduction control measures, instead of actually controlling their pollution. Furthermore, the bill provides no guidelines or oversight for how regulatory bodies should use such funds to ``maximize emissions reductions in the area.''
This subsection also establishes that the bill's preferential treatment solely applies to advanced manufacturing facilities--those involved in semiconductor manufacturing--and critical mineral facilities--those involved in the extraction, processing, refining, or milling of critical minerals (as designated by the Secretary of the Interior). All other industries and facilities would be forced to cut more pollution to make up for the provisions of this bill.
CONCLUSION
Despite the majority's claims, H.R. 6373 is nothing more than a polluter handout and pay-to-play scheme for the most well connected. Despite attempts by Committee Democrats, Republicans failed to address the fundamental flaws in the bill, putting the health of Americans at risk.
For the reasons stated above, we dissent from the views contained in the Committee's report.
Frank Pallone, Jr.,
Ranking Member.
